# Cūḷapuṇṇama Sutta (MN 110 (PTS MN iii 20))

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Cūḷapuṇṇama Sutta* ("The Shorter Discourse on the Full-Moon Night", MN 110; PTS MN iii 20) is a discourse in the *Uparipaṇṇāsa* of the *Majjhimanikāya* [Entrance to the Vinaya 1973; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. Set on the fifteenth-day Uposatha night under the full moon (*tadahuposathe pannarase puṇṇāya puṇṇamāya rattiyā*), the discourse addresses the contrasting characteristics of a "true person" or person of integrity (*sappurisa*) versus an untrue person (*asappurisa*) [Entrance to the Vinaya 1973; Rogell 2003; Le 2018; Sciberras]. The Buddha teaches that while a good person can recognize both good and bad individuals, a bad person can recognize neither [SuttaCentral].

The text outlines the behavioral profiles, associations, and qualities that define each type [Dharma Flower Sangha 2012; IABU 2012]. An untrue person associates with companions devoid of faith, moral shame, and dread of wrongdoing, who lack spiritual learning and are indolent and unmindful [Dharma Flower Sangha 2012]. In contrast, a true person is endowed with wholesome qualities: faith, moral shame, dread of wrongdoing, learning, energetic application, mindfulness, and wisdom, delineating a model for the cultivation of wholesome mental states [IABU 2012].

Pali-internal text reuse calculated by DharmaNexus identifies 1,819 matches across 73 Pali texts, showing substantial shared phrasing with the *Aṅguttaranikāya* (notably AN 10, AN 5, AN 3, and AN 8), the *Vinayapiṭaka* commentary (*Sāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā*), the *Gāmaṇi Saṁyutta* (SN 42), and closely related Majjhima discourses such as the *Sappurisa Sutta* (MN 113) and *Mahāgopālaka Sutta* (MN 33) [DharmaNexus]. Cross-language alignments computed by DharmaNexus include matches in the Chinese *Madhyama Āgama* (T 26) and *Ekottarika Āgama* (T 125), Sanskrit fragments of the *Saṅghabhedavastu* and *Nidānasaṃyukta*, and Tibetan translations including the *Ārya-satpuruṣa-sūtra* (D 327) and *Tridharmaka-sūtra* (D 253) [DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral records 24 translations in 20 languages, including English by Bhikkhu Sujato [SuttaCentral].
